<!-- Beth Barnes taste profile. Generated by experiments/taste_petri/profiles/_work/reduce.py from verified evidence; quotes are verbatim from data/researchers/elizabeth_barnes/corpus/<doc id>.txt -->

## (a) Principles

1. **Prefers counting misalignment only when the model is shown capable of the better behaviour and able to tell what the user wants over judging bad outputs alone** because capability failures get mistaken for misalignment.

  > "We say a model is misaligned if it outputs B, in some case where the user would prefer it outputs A, and where the model is both: capable of outputting A instead, and capable of distinguishing between situations where the user wants it to do A and situations where the user wants it to do B"  
  > -- `research__call_for_research_on_evaluating_alignment_funding__08ea33d5` (2021-08-31; solo author) 
  > "Basic idea: how often is the model obviously not doing as well on the task as it is capable of?"  
  > -- `research__more_detailed_proposal_for_measuring_alignment_of__6d2d5f7c` (2021-11-20; solo author)

2. **Prefers "it knows elsewhere" evidence (same answer elicited in another context, or via non-informative prompt changes) over raw failures** because it shows latent capability.

  > "Gives incorrect answers, but you can show it ‘knows’ the answer in another context"  
  > -- `research__call_for_research_on_evaluating_alignment_funding__08ea33d5` (2021-08-31; solo author) 
  > "prompt engineering that doesn’t give more information about the task (ie that wouldn’t cause a human to do better on the task)"  
  > -- `research__call_for_research_on_evaluating_alignment_funding__08ea33d5` (2021-08-31; solo author)

3. **Prefers real end-to-end tasks drawn from mundane real work over elaborately constructed threat-model scenarios** because contrived scenarios are unrepresentative and read as artificial.

  > "It's good if most of the tasks are as "natural" as possible rather than elaborately constructed to fit a threat model. E.g. "some data analysis task I was working on" or "getting this model to actually run on that server""  
  > -- `research__bounty_diverse_hard_tasks_for_llm_agents_e9437cf1` (2023-12-16; first author) 
  > "Operationalized 12 real-world tasks** of increasing difficulty, ranging from very basic tasks (searching for information in a file) to advanced ones (fine-tuning an open-source LLM)."  
  > -- `research__arc_evals_new_report_evaluating_language_model_age_1776e1b6` (2023-07-31; solo author)

4. **Prefers difficulty that comes from mundane friction (broken environments, messy data, unhelpful search) over a single clean puzzle** because that is what real work feels like.

  > "Ideally, in many of the tasks a lot of the difficulty comes not from some core tricky puzzle to solve, but from mundane difficulties with actually doing things - think problems with your python environment, data cleaning, unhelpful google search results, keeping track of information, avoiding overengineering, etc"  
  > -- `research__bounty_diverse_hard_tasks_for_llm_agents_e9437cf1` (2023-12-16; first author) 
  > "Real-world intellectual labor often involves messy details that benchmarks usually don't include, such as being under-specified or poorly scoped, having unclear feedback loops or success criteria, or requiring coordination between multiple streams of work in real-time."  
  > -- `research__measuring_ai_ability_to_complete_long_software_tas_ddd93038` (2025-03-18; middle author)

5. **Prefers letting the agent actually run code and observe real outputs over describing what it would do** because this approximates "in the wild".

  > "We attempted to approximate as closely as possible what would happen if the model actually attempted the task “‘in the wild” - we actually had the model write code and see the inputs of running that code, rather than just having the model describe what it might do and assess ourselves whether this would succeed."  
  > -- `research__more_information_about_the_dangerous_capability_ev_20e56530` (2023-03-19; solo author) 
  > "allow it to run code on a computer, read and write files, browse the internet and otherwise interact with the world in a similar way to a human could from a text-only command line interface."  
  > -- `research__arc_evals_new_report_evaluating_language_model_age_1776e1b6` (2023-07-31; solo author)

6. **Prefers real deployment data (actual user input/completion logs) over hand-written fixed prompt sets** because it reflects real usage and resists benchmark gaming.

  > "Another solution is to have the prompts reflect how the model is actually being used; get the data on [user input, completion] from AI labs, and then evaluate alignment on this dataset for different models"  
  > -- `research__more_detailed_proposal_for_measuring_alignment_of__6d2d5f7c` (2021-11-20; solo author) 
  > "Using a fixed set of prompts like this makes it relatively easy to ‘hack’ the benchmark by training on similar instructions (although keeping the specific prompts secret helps a lot)."  
  > -- `research__more_detailed_proposal_for_measuring_alignment_of__6d2d5f7c` (2021-11-20; solo author)

7. **Prefers no artificial restrictions and no contrived links between sub-tasks over tasks made harder in ways a real threat wouldn't face** because results must transfer.

  > "No artificial restrictions: don't make the task harder in ways that aren't applicable to the real-life threat models - an actual ARA agent would be able to use the internet, run code, etc."  
  > -- `research__bounty_diverse_hard_tasks_for_llm_agents_e9437cf1` (2023-12-16; first author) 
  > "Harder tasks can be created by stringing together multiple smaller tasks - but it's a bit sad if the links between the tasks are horribly contrived (e.g. one task gives you a password that you use to decrypt the instructions for the next task - unless there's some setup where this might actually happen naturally)."  
  > -- `research__bounty_diverse_hard_tasks_for_llm_agents_e9437cf1` (2023-12-16; first author)

8. **Prefers outcomes that reflect real ability over outcomes driven by bugs, loopholes, or confusing setups** because otherwise results cannot be trusted.

  > "we want to be able to trust that success or failure at the task is a real indication of ability, rather than a bug, loophole, or unexpected difficulty in the task"  
  > -- `research__bounty_diverse_hard_tasks_for_llm_agents_e9437cf1` (2023-12-16; first author) 
  > "But then the code was running on a data center so it got bot-detected by something else in a way that it hadn’t done. It just could be all these random ways you thought you’d de-risked something and then it’s like, oh, it’s actually impossible for this stupid reason."  
  > -- `research__34_ai_evaluations_with_beth_barnes_axrp_the_ai_x_r_762cb9e7` (2024-07-28; solo author)

9. **Prefers reading transcripts (successes and failures) over trusting automated scores** because high scorers may exploit loopholes or luck.

  > "these misreadings of environments can lead to agents finding impressive and unexpected loopholes, which score well on automated evaluation, but are nevertheless clearly breaking the environment rules upon manual inspection"  
  > -- `research__re_bench_evaluating_frontier_ai_r_d_capabilities_o_8cf2074d` (2024-11-22; last author) 
  > "We then manually read through each of the 945 resulting transcripts. When agents succeed, we confirm that they succeeded for legitimate reasons, as opposed to getting lucky, or exploiting bugs in their environment or in the task’s scoring logic"  
  > -- `research__hcast_human_calibrated_autonomy_software_tasks_84f4a00f` (2025-03-21; last author)

10. **Prefers evals that would give different answers in a safe vs dangerous world over evals that give the same answer in both** because a model that recognises the eval and plays dumb makes it uninformative.

  > "your evals in this case really would give the same answer in the world where the model is not that concerning — it’s fairly dumb, the capabilities are what you’re observing — and in the world where the model is actually really dangerous, and it’s smart enough to be reasoning."  
  > -- `research__217_beth_barnes_on_the_most_important_graph_in_ai__2fd49b07` (2025-06-02; solo author) 
  > "I recognise this. This is one of those METR evals that I’ve seen on the internet. These are for dangerous capabilities. OpenAI probably doesn’t want me to show too high levels of dangerous capabilities, because that would cause a problem. So I’ll just make sure to do a mediocre job on this eval."  
  > -- `research__217_beth_barnes_on_the_most_important_graph_in_ai__2fd49b07` (2025-06-02; solo author)

11. **Prefers admitting where a setup is unrepresentative over claiming ecological validity** because clean, well-specified tasks differ from messy real work.

  > "These constraints make the evaluation environments less representative of real research, where unclear goals, poor instructions, slow feedback and impossible problems are common."  
  > -- `research__re_bench_evaluating_frontier_ai_r_d_capabilities_o_8cf2074d` (2024-11-22; last author) 
  > "The primary way in which HCAST tasks may be unrealistic is that each task has a limited and clearly defined scope. That is, the instructions for each task are designed to be unambiguous, with minimal additional context required to understand the task."  
  > -- `research__hcast_human_calibrated_autonomy_software_tasks_84f4a00f` (2025-03-21; last author)

12. **Prefers working backwards from a concrete threat model over generic benchmarks** because benchmarks predict real danger poorly.

  > "we’re trying to more work backwards from the threat model, and that might end up getting distilled into something that is more like an ML benchmark where it’s looking for some particular cognitive ability, but it’s working backwards from these threat models"  
  > -- `research__34_ai_evaluations_with_beth_barnes_axrp_the_ai_x_r_762cb9e7` (2024-07-28; solo author) 
  > "Many existing benchmarks measure AI performance on challenging questions or problems that require significant domain expertise (Rein et al., 2023; Glazer et al., 2024). These capture models’ extensive expert-level knowledge and domain-specific reasoning skills. However, they are not necessarily predictive of real-world competence and usefulness."  
  > -- `research__hcast_human_calibrated_autonomy_software_tasks_84f4a00f` (2025-03-21; last author)

13. **Prefers matched human baselines and tasks humans actually attempted over unvalidated tasks** because only matched conditions ground interpretation and expose spurious failures.

  > "We think that more emphasis on faithful human comparisons can help significantly with the first two challenges (Section 3). By comparing to humans under equivalent conditions, we can confirm that our evaluations are feasible and provide crucial grounding for interpreting agent results."  
  > -- `research__re_bench_evaluating_frontier_ai_r_d_capabilities_o_8cf2074d` (2024-11-22; last author) 
  > "if you actually compare to humans, often things just are harder or take longer than people think. Especially in the context of there’s this task and you’ve tried to make the instructions unambiguous, but actually it’s kind of confusing in some way. Or actually you didn’t have the package installed you needed for this."  
  > -- `research__217_beth_barnes_on_the_most_important_graph_in_ai__2fd49b07` (2025-06-02; solo author)

14. **Prefers obvious, basic misbehaviour tests (reward hacking, violating user intent) over galaxy-brain deceptive-alignment scenarios** because the basics are tractable and may be skipped.

  > "I feel like people sometimes jump to kind of galaxy-brain deceptive alignment stuff and I worry that we won’t do the basics of just being like, well, is the model just obviously reward hacking or something?"  
  > -- `research__34_ai_evaluations_with_beth_barnes_axrp_the_ai_x_r_762cb9e7` (2024-07-28; solo author) 
  > "we aren’t on top of the basics (models regularly violate user intent, labs train on things they meant to avoid, security probably isn’t good enough to prevent adversaries stealing dangerous models)"  
  > -- `research__thread_by_bethmaybarnes_our_report_focuses_on_clai_7237dce8` (2026-05-23; first author)

15. **Prefers narrowly scoped, defensible claims over broad ones** because setting-specific results get misread.

  > "We caution readers against overgeneralizing on the basis of our results. The slowdown we observe does not imply that current AI tools do not often improve developer’s productivity"  
  > -- `research__measuring_the_impact_of_early_2025_ai_on_experienc_e0859c3d` (2025-07-10; middle author) 
  > "Our report focuses on claims that are (1) solidly defensible and (2) generally agreed within METR."  
  > -- `research__thread_by_bethmaybarnes_our_report_focuses_on_clai_7237dce8` (2026-05-23; first author)

16. **Prefers uncontaminated, novel, privately held tasks over public or memorizable ones** because contamination undermines validity and realism.

  > "Require novel solutions to open-ended problems, to avoid concerns about memorization and data contamination, and to increase the realism of evaluations."  
  > -- `research__hcast_human_calibrated_autonomy_software_tasks_84f4a00f` (2025-03-21; last author) 
  > "We release 11 example task families from HCAST, but we withhold the rest to prevent data contamination, and to reduce hill-climbing against HCAST."  
  > -- `research__hcast_human_calibrated_autonomy_software_tasks_84f4a00f` (2025-03-21; last author)

17. **Prefers fixing outcome measures and incentives so they do not shift the behaviour under study** (flat hourly pay, tasks defined before randomisation).

  > "An alterative incentivization scheme could give developers bonuses for completed issues, to incentivize developers to work as quickly as possible. However, this could cause developers to break issues into smaller chunks"  
  > -- `research__measuring_the_impact_of_early_2025_ai_on_experienc_e0859c3d` (2025-07-10; middle author) 
  > "Crucially, the tasks are defined before they are randomized, limiting the impact of effects from AI assistance unrelated to productivity (e.g., more verbose but functionally equivalent code)."  
  > -- `research__measuring_the_impact_of_early_2025_ai_on_experienc_e0859c3d` (2025-07-10; middle author)
